title: Question 5
stem:
A capacitor of capacitance $470\,\mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) $24\text{ V}$ in the circuit of Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The two-way switch S is initially at position X.

P and Q are identical long straight wires, each with a resistance of $5.6\text{ k}\Omega$. These wires are placed near to, and parallel to, each other. Wire Q is connected to a voltmeter.

At time $t = 0$, switch S is moved to position Y so that the capacitor discharges through wire P.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the charge $Q_0$ on the capacitor at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the capacitor after it has been connected to position X for a long time - what p.d. must be across its plates just before t = 0?
Hint 2: Remember how charge, capacitance and p.d. are linked, and first convert $470\,\mu\text{F}$ to farads ($1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the fully charged state**
You are sitting with the switch at X for a long time before t = 0. That means the capacitor has finished charging. Its plates must be at the same p.d. as the battery, so $V_0 = 24\text{ V}$. No current flows once it is full.

Step 2: **Use capacitance to get charge**
Capacitance tells you how much charge is stored per volt: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$ so $$Q_0 = C V_0$$ Put $C = 470\,\mu\text{F} = 470 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$ and $V_0 = 24\text{ V}$: $$Q_0 = (470 \times 10^{-6}) \times 24 = 1.13 \times 10^{-2}\text{ C} \approx 0.011\text{ C}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the current $I_0$ in wire P at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: At the instant the switch moves to Y, the capacitor with its full 24 V is suddenly connected across wire P of resistance $5.6\text{ k}\Omega$ - what drives the first surge of current?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Ohm's law at t = 0**
At t = 0 the whole capacitor voltage appears across P. Think of the capacitor as a 24 V supply for that instant. With $R = 5.6\text{ k}\Omega = 5600\,\Omega$: $$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R} = \frac{24}{5600} = 4.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$$ This is the maximum current, it only falls after this.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the time constant $\tau$ of the discharge circuit.
hints: Hint 1: The speed of a capacitor discharge is set by both how much charge it holds and how hard it is for current to flow - which two circuit values from Fig. 5.1 control this?
Hint 2: Combine resistance in ohms and capacitance in farads to get the time constant in seconds, remembering to convert $\text{k}\Omega$ and $\mu\text{F}$ to base SI units.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what time constant means**
$\tau$ is the characteristic time for discharge. A big resistance slows the current and a big capacitance stores more charge, so both make discharge slower.

Step 2: **Calculate RC**
$$\tau = R C$$ Use $R = 5.6\text{ k}\Omega = 5600\,\Omega$ and $C = 470 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$: $$\tau = 5600 \times 470 \times 10^{-6} = 2.63\text{ s} \approx 2.6\text{ s}$$ After one time constant the current and charge have fallen to about 37% of their starting values.

parts.label: (a)(iv)

markscheme_points.text: line with negative gradient throughout passing through $(0, I_0)$

hints: Hint 1: Think about how the discharge current changes - is it fastest at the start when voltage is high, and what happens to the rate of fall as voltage drops?
Hint 2: Remember the shape is not a straight line - the gradient must get less steep with time but never quite reach zero current.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at $(0, I_0)$ on the $I$-axis, falling steeply at first then ever less steeply, asymptotic to the $t$-axis. Exponential decay with negative gradient throughout.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start at maximum**
At $t = 0$, $I = I_0$ from (a)(ii). So your line must pass through the marked $I_0$ on the vertical axis. This is the highest point.

Step 2: **Draw exponential decay**
As charge leaves, $V$ falls, so $I = V/R$ also falls, which in turn slows the loss of charge. That feedback gives: $$I = I_0 e^{-t/RC}$$ Draw a smooth curve with negative gradient everywhere, steepest at $t = 0$ and flattening out, getting closer and closer to the $t$-axis but never touching it.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain why there is an induced e.m.f. across wire Q during the discharge of the capacitor.

markscheme_points.text: current in wire P gives rise to a magnetic field
as current (in P) changes, wire Q cuts (magnetic) flux (of wire P)
cutting magnetic flux causes induced e.m.f. (across Q)

hints: Hint 1: Start with wire P alone - what surrounds any long straight wire while a current flows in it?
Hint 2: Now think about what is special during discharge - the current in P is not steady but falling exponentially, so what is happening to that surrounding effect at the position of Q?
Hint 3: Link a changing magnetic environment at Q to Faraday's law - what is induced in a conductor that experiences changing flux?
parts.proper_answer: Current in P produces a magnetic field. As P discharges the current changes, so the magnetic flux linking nearby wire Q changes / Q cuts changing flux. By Faraday's law a changing flux induces an e.m.f. across Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Field from P**
Any current creates magnetic field lines around the wire. So while discharge current flows in P, there is a magnetic field in the space around it, including where Q sits.

Step 2: **Changing flux at Q**
During discharge the current in P is falling rapidly. Therefore its magnetic field is also weakening and changing with time. Wire Q, placed parallel and close to P, experiences a changing magnetic flux linkage.

Step 3: **Induce e.m.f.**
Faraday's law says a changing magnetic flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in a conductor. So even though Q is not connected to the capacitor, the changing field from P induces an e.m.f. across Q, which the voltmeter detects.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: sketch shows line with a negative gradient throughout

hints: Hint 1: The voltmeter reads the induced e.m.f., which depends on how fast the current in P is changing - when is that rate of change largest and how does it evolve?
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at a maximum $V$ at $t=0$ and falling smoothly to zero, with negative gradient throughout (same exponential decay shape as current).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow the rate of change**
Induced e.m.f. is proportional to rate of change of current, $V \propto dI/dt$. For exponential decay the gradient $dI/dt$ is largest in magnitude at $t = 0$ and then its magnitude shrinks toward zero. So $V$ is maximum at $t = 0$ and decays toward zero with a negative gradient throughout, mirroring the decay in (a)(iv).
